## 1. Statement

We prove rigorously:

> **Theorem.** \(\sqrt{2}\) is irrational.

Equivalently, there do not exist integers \(p\) and \(q \neq 0\) such that

\[
\sqrt{2}=\frac{p}{q}.
\]

---

## 2. A useful theorem: Euclid’s lemma and unique factorization

The standard proof uses the following theorem.

### Euclid’s Lemma

If \(p\) is a prime number and

\[
p \mid ab,
\]

then

\[
p \mid a \quad \text{or} \quad p \mid b.
\]

Here \(p \mid a\) means that \(p\) divides \(a\).

For the special case \(p=2\), Euclid’s lemma says:

> If \(2 \mid ab\), then \(2 \mid a\) or \(2 \mid b\).

In particular, if

\[
2 \mid a^2,
\]

then taking \(b=a\), we get

\[
2 \mid a.
\]

This is the key idea: an even square must come from an even number.

---

### Why Euclid’s lemma is true

One standard proof uses Bézout’s identity.

If \(\gcd(p,a)=1\), then there exist integers \(x,y\) such that

\[
px+ay=1.
\]

Multiply by \(b\):

\[
pbx+aby=b.
\]

Now suppose \(p \mid ab\). Then \(p \mid ab\), and of course \(p \mid pbx\). Therefore \(p\) divides their sum:

\[
p \mid pbx+aby=b.
\]

Thus if \(p\) does not divide \(a\), then \(\gcd(p,a)=1\), so \(p \mid b\). Therefore

\[
p \mid a \quad \text{or} \quad p \mid b.
\]

This proves Euclid’s lemma.

A closely related theorem is the **Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic**, which says that every integer greater than \(1\) has a unique prime factorization. Euclid’s lemma is one of the basic facts that makes unique prime factorization work.

---

\[
\sqrt{2}=\frac{a}{b}.
\]

\[
\gcd(a,b)=1.
\]

\[

\[

\[
